passage: The export order at the Ludhiana factory was due by Friday. When the stitching line fell behind again, Pankaj kicked a stool so hard it split, then stood over a young trainee, shouting inches from her face. She shrank back against the wall. Hemant had seen this before: the punched locker, the phone thrown at the wall, people going quiet when Pankaj walked in. This wasn't a bad day. It was a pattern. Hemant stepped between them, calm but firm. "Pankaj, step outside. Now." He walked the trainee to the supervisor's office and told the supervisor everything. The supervisor moved her to another line and said a formal warning would follow. At the end of the shift Hemant found Pankaj alone by the gate. "Bhai, people are scared of you. The company has a counsellor. I think you should see them." Pankaj stared at the split stool and said nothing for a long time.

qa.a: Pankaj kicked a stool so hard it split.

qa.q: In what order did Hemant act, and why?
qa.a: Hemant put safety first by stepping in and taking the trainee to the supervisor, then later urged Pankaj privately to see the company counsellor.

qa.q: What might Pankaj be feeling as he stares at the split stool?
qa.a: Pankaj may be feeling shaken or ashamed, perhaps seeing the damage clearly for the first time, though he says nothing.

passage: The dent in the bathroom door of the Nagpur flat was new. So was the crack across the TV screen. Kishore noticed both when he came for Sunday lunch, and he noticed how his sister-in-law Rekha flinched when his elder brother Manoj raised his voice about the rice. The children slipped away to their room. Kishore had grown up with Manoj's temper, but this was different: constant, and people were afraid. That evening, when Manoj started shouting and slammed a plate onto the table, Kishore quietly took Rekha and the children down to a neighbour's flat and stayed with them. Rekha decided to spend the week at her sister's. The next morning, with Manoj calm, Kishore sat across from him. "Bhaiya, the door, the TV, the kids hiding. This isn't just stress. I've found a counsellor who works with anger. I'll come with you to the first session." Manoj stared at his hands. "Okay," he said at last.

qa.q: What new damage did Kishore notice in the flat?
qa.a: A dent in the bathroom door and a crack across the TV screen.

qa.q: What did Kishore conclude about Manoj's temper, and how did he feel?
qa.a: Kishore was worried; he saw that it was no longer just stress but a constant pattern that made people afraid.

qa.q: Why did Kishore wait until the next morning to talk to Manoj?
qa.a: Safety came first that evening, so the family left the flat; talking once Manoj was calm gave a better chance that he would listen.

qa.q: What is it like for Rekha and the children to live with Manoj's outbursts?
qa.a: They seem frightened; Rekha flinches at his raised voice and the children slip away to their room.

'Zubin, can we talk? Outside, not at the desks.'
'If it's about the printer, I've said sorry.'
Lalremsiami kept her voice level. 'It's not only the printer. Last week you threw the stapler. On Monday you shouted in Rina's face until she cried. She asked me whether she could move floors.'
'Everyone here makes me angry. The deadlines are insane.'
'The deadlines are insane for all of us. But I'm seeing this almost every week, and people are scared of you. That's not a bad mood any more.'
Zubin stared at the car park. 'I don't even remember deciding to throw things.'
'I've told our manager so Rina can sit with another team for now. And the company has a counsellor. I think you should see them this week.'
A long silence. 'Will you send me the number?'
'Sending it now.'

passage: The first time Charu threw her phone, I laughed it off. We'd shared the flat for a year, and she'd always had a temper. Then it was the bathroom door, slammed so hard the frame cracked. Then a steel plate hurled at the wall, a foot from my head, because I'd used her milk. Each time she apologised the next morning, cheerful again. I started tiptoeing around my own home and checking her mood before I spoke. One night, lying awake with my heart racing, I finally admitted it: this wasn't a bad mood. It was a pattern, and I was scared. The next evening I slept at a friend's place. Then I met Charu at a café and told her, calmly, that I couldn't live with it and that she needed to see a counsellor. She cried. A week later she showed me her appointment card. I'm Ishita, and I'm still learning to trust that flat again.

qa.q: What did Charu throw at the wall?
qa.a: A steel plate.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel living with Charu before that night?
qa.a: Ishita felt scared and on edge, tiptoeing around the flat and checking Charu's mood before speaking.

qa.q: What made Ishita's response sensible?
qa.a: Ishita put personal safety first by staying at a friend's place, then spoke calmly in a public place and pushed for a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when Ishita spoke to her at the café?
qa.a: Charu was probably ashamed and upset, which may have helped her take the step of booking an appointment.

passage:
Football club note, Saturday
Today, for the third match running, our assistant coach Suraj lost his temper with the under-twelves. After a missed pass he kicked the water crate across the bench and shouted into Aarush's face from very close. Aarush went pale and two other children started crying. I stopped the session, moved the children to the far goal with the second coach, and asked Suraj to leave the ground for the day. Before home time I reported it to the club's welfare officer, who phoned Aarush's parents that evening and met me and Suraj the next morning. Suraj told us he doesn't know why it keeps happening, and that it scares him too. He has agreed to see a counsellor and will not coach until he has. The children will get a calm debrief at Tuesday's practice.
Tanuja, head coach

qa.q: What did Suraj kick across the bench?
qa.a: The water crate.

qa.q: What does Suraj saying 'it scares him too' suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels frightened and ashamed of his own outbursts and does not understand why they keep happening.

qa.q: Why was it right to move the children before dealing with Suraj?
qa.a: The children's safety came first; only once they were away from him could Tanuja deal with the pattern and report it.

qa.q: How might Aarush and the other children see Suraj now?
qa.a: They are probably scared of him and may need calm reassurance before they feel safe at practice again.

grounding: Shows a head coach who sees repeated explosions and intimidation by a young coach, puts the children's safety first, reports it and arranges counselling.

Thursday night
Third time this month. Vasudha slammed her laptop shut in the design review, then threw a stapler that dented the wall right next to Kunal's head. Nobody said anything; everyone just stared at their screens. The new intern was shaking. I kept telling myself it's only stress, she's brilliant, she'll calm down. But this isn't a bad mood any more. People are scared of her.
After lunch I went to Meenakshi, our manager, and told her what I'd seen, including the stapler. She listened, thanked me, moved the intern to another desk that same afternoon, and said she'd speak to Vasudha tomorrow about safety and about seeing the company counsellor. I feel sick about it, but also relieved.
Jyoti

qa.a: A stapler, which dented the wall next to Kunal's head.

qa.a: Jyoti feels sick about it but also relieved, torn between loyalty to a colleague and everyone's safety.
